newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Renault to axe jobs in France.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Renault to axe jobs in France.

text.p: Ailing French car group Renault SA, facing big losses and shrinking demand for its vehicles, told its works council on Tuesday it plans to cut 2,764 jobs in France this year on top of a fiercely contested plant closure in Belgium.

Angry trade union leaders warned the company it could face a long labour conflict over the cuts, while a senior French government parliamentarian accused Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer of acting over-hastily and called for negotiations.

The job cut plan for France follows last Thursday's decision to close the Renault plant at Vilvoorde near Brussels in June, with the loss of 3,100 direct jobs and another 1,000 more at risk at supplying companies.
It was contained in information handed out to works council members ahead of a meeting with management on Thursday, union sources said. Renault has a total workforce of 140,000.
A Renault spokeswoman declined comment on the cuts but said the central staff committee would be meeting on March 13 to discuss an "employment plan" in France.

The programme would include "both a labour restructuring with internal transfers and the elimination of posts, as well as measures aimed at youth employment, with new recruitment to make up for early retirements," she said.
The cuts, if carried through, would be the biggest by the partially privatised company since it shed 3,700 jobs in 1992 when still state-owned. The French state still retains a 46 percent stake.
Renault unions have called a one-hour strike on Friday in all plants in France, Belgium and Spain to protest against the shutdown of the Belgian factory.
"We hope this is the beginning of a long period of labour struggle at Renault all over Europe," Daniel Richter of the pro-Socialist CFDT union said on Europe 1 radio on Tuesday.

Senior government parliamentarian Michel Pericard criticised the way the Vilvoorde decision was announced and urged Schweitzer to open negotiations with the workforce and the government on an early retirement plan rejected by the industry ministry last week.
"This decision was a surprise and a shock. There is no reason why things should be so sudden and brutal without anyone being consulted or prepared," he told RTL radio.

Renault officials rejected the criticism, saying there was no "nice way" to break such news and insisting the job cuts, which they said had been delayed due to the slow privatisation process, were vital to make Renault competitive.

Renault, privatised in stages in 1994 and 1996, is expected to announce on March 20 a 1996 operating loss of more than two billion francs ($347 million) as well as a 2.4 billion franc exceptional charge for the Belgian restructuring and possibly other job-cutting costs.

Pericard, National Assembly floor leader of President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, said he was sure the government would reconsider a plan proposed jointly by Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen to retire 40,000 car workers aged over 51, if it was sure it would lead to the recruitment of young job-seekers.
Union leaders complained they had been neither consulted nor informed about the closure of the plant in Vilvoorde, the home town of Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene.

"This is an unacceptable method and has produced entirely justified reactions. It is unworthy of Renault," said Philippe Martinez, an official of the communist-led CGT union, the largest at Renault. "It's obviously just the start of a mobilisation against job cuts."

The Flanders regional government has said it will sue Renault for allegedly failing to respect European labour law over the closure of Vilvoorde. But a senior Renault executive said on Tuesday he saw no legal basis for such a suit.
"My feeling is that we have completely respected all the procedures," said Michel de Virville, senior vice-president in charge of personnel and external relations.
He told reporters at the Geneva Car Show the closure did not reflect the quality of work at the plant but was essential for the group's industrial strategy.
